From spectators gathering for a flag-raising at a new Cenotaph in 1968 to veterans marching to city hall for a Korean War plaque dedication in 1994, Williams Lake has a long tradition of honouring those who served – one that continues. The Williams Lake and District Cenotaph was built in 1968 below the former War Memorial Hospital, a joint undertaking by the municipality and Royal Canadian Legion Branch 139 to honour the area’s war dead, according to the Veterans Affairs Canada’s website. The Cariboo War Memorial Hospital opened in May 1925, partly funded by the community of Soda Creek to honour fallen First World War soldiers. In 1968, the _Williams Lake Tribune_ reported on spectators gathering for a flag-raising ceremony at the new monument. Sixteen years later, the cenotaph was moved beside city hall and rededicated on Nov. 3, 1984, in conjunction with the dedication of the new municipal building. Days after the cenotaph’s rededication beside city hall, the _Tribune’s_ Nov. 8, 1984 edition outlined the plans for that year’s Remembrance Day Observance, bringing together veterans, students and community groups. The service began at 10:45 a.m. at the Elks Hall on Nov. 11, 1984 with the Williams Lake Community Band playing O Canada and a student from Anne Stevenson Junior Secondary School’s drama class reading In Flanders Field. Bill Lannigan and A.E McMath read the names of the former residents who died in the First and Second World Wars, followed by the Last Post and two minutes of silence. After the service, Legion members, RCMP, Sea Cadets, Air Cadets and youth organizations included Cubs, Scouts, Voyageurs, Guides and Brownies paraded to the cenotaph for wreath-laying, before returning to the Legion hall to lay wreaths at its cairn. It is Paraguay’s largest private investment but local people accuse a forestry giant of ignoring their contamination concerns over its vast plantation

When Paracel arrived in Tacuarita, an Indigenous community of homes made from planks and plastic sheeting in Paraguay’s poorest region, six years ago, it was a welcome sight. The company improved the dirt roads and dug an electric-powered well, saving villagers a two-mile journey to fetch water from a cattle pond that often made them sick. It also gave dozens of local people forestry jobs.

“They fulfilled all their promises,” says Florencio Garcete, 55, chief of the Mbya Guaraní community of 211 people.

items.title: [americanagnetwork.com] USDA cuts corn yield, tightens soybean stocks, lifts grain prices
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) cut its 2026/27 U.S. corn yield estimate to 179.6 bushels per acre in its Nov. 10 World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates report, lowering projected production by 141 million bushels to 15.893 billion. Soybean yield edged up to 53.3 bushels per acre, but a higher export forecast reduced projected ending stocks by 15 million bushels to 300 million. The tighter-than-expected estimates lifted grain futures: December corn rose nearly 12 cents to $4.51 a bushel, and January soybeans gained more than 35 cents to above $12.24 during Tuesday trading. USDA also lowered its corn export forecast by 25 million bushels and raised its soybean export forecast by the same amount. With most U.S. production estimates now set until USDA’s January update, traders are watching export demand and South American crop weather.

items.title: [ja.se] European farm groups seek exemption from energy rationing during shortages
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Copa-Cogeca, an umbrella group for European farm organizations and cooperatives, has urged the European Commission and EU member states to exempt agriculture and food production from any energy restrictions imposed during a shortage. In a letter sent ahead of an EU energy ministers’ meeting scheduled for Oct. 29, it said farming and food processing depend on reliable supplies of electricity, gas and fuel. The group also called for a coordinated EU approach to high energy and diesel prices, arguing that differing national support measures could distort competition between farmers. It wants better rural grid connections, simpler permits and greater access to financing to help farms produce renewable energy. It also supports greater use of sustainably produced European biofuels to reduce reliance on imported fossil fuels.

items.title: [eos.org] Arctic ice cores trace century-old toxic pollution to Montana mine
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Researchers traced arsenic and other heavy metals preserved in 10 Arctic ice cores to the Anaconda Copper Mine in Montana, linking pollution to a single industrial source thousands of kilometers away. Arsenic levels in some cores reached about 15 times preindustrial levels around 1914, according to the study in Nature Sustainability. By combining ice-core measurements, atmospheric modeling and historical production records, the team estimated that about 50.5 million Americans and 600,000 Canadians were exposed to arsenic levels associated with increased health risks between 1898 and 1918. Pollution-control equipment installed at the smelter in 1919 reduced emissions by roughly 60% to 65%, though the mine continued operating until 1947. Lead researcher Joseph McConnell, a climate and environmental scientist at the Desert Research Institute, said epidemiologists should investigate the pollution’s potential effects on people.

An exceptionally strong 2026–27 El Niño is disrupting food production and prompting emergency measures. Peru declared an emergency across more than 70% of its municipalities over flood danger, with authorities warning that more than 9 million people face a high risk of floods and landslides. In the Philippines, unmilled rice production fell 18% in the three months to September, while forecasters expect below-normal rainfall in November. Nearly 896,000 hectares have burned in Indonesia since January; smoke has led to school closures and respiratory illness, according to a report citing BBC. Cereal maker Kellanova has also changed the ingredients in Rice Krispies and Coco Pops sold in the UK and Europe, citing weather-related problems with the availability and quality of rice and grains. The UN’s International Fund for Agricultural Development (IFAD) says overlapping climate and economic shocks could cost the global economy as much as $11 trillion, with energy and fertilizer costs adding pressure across food systems. The UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said in September it had received only one-fifth of the $202 million requested to prepare for food crises in 22 high-risk countries.

items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

El Niño-related peat fires and forest degradation in Southeast Asia are projected to push land-use carbon emissions higher in 2026, bringing total global CO₂ emissions to 43.3 billion tonnes even as fossil-fuel emissions edge down, according to the Global Carbon Project’s annual assessment. The researchers link the rise in land-use emissions to drier conditions and fires often ignited by human activity. The 21st Global Carbon Budget, published Nov. 10 in Earth System Science Data and presented during the U.N. climate conference in Antalya, projects 5.1 billion tonnes of emissions from land-use change this year. The projected decline in fossil-fuel emissions is partly attributable to the Iran conflict’s energy shock, alongside the growing contribution of solar, wind and electric vehicles. The report says the land carbon sink recovered in 2025 after weakening during the 2023-24 El Niño, but the strong 2026 El Niño is expected to weaken it again in 2027. Separately, an analysis of Chinese data found that emissions fell 3.1% in July-September, the country’s steepest quarterly drop since pandemic lockdowns in 2022.

items.title: [thesouthafrican.com] WMO warns strengthening El Niño could intensify global extremes into 2027
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) says a strengthening El Niño could reach record strength by December and intensify heat and disruptive rainfall patterns into 2027. In its 2026 climate update, the agency reported that global temperatures from January through September averaged about 1.47°C above the preindustrial level and said 2026 is on track to rank among the four warmest years on record. items.title: [proplanta.de] EU convenes crisis talks as freezer hacks spread to Germany, Romania
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

The European Commission convened two crisis meetings after cyberattacks on supermarket refrigeration systems spread across Europe, with incidents reported in at least 11 countries, including Germany and Romania. The attacks remotely raised temperatures or triggered defrost cycles, forcing retailers to discard food; no group has claimed responsibility, and authorities have not established whether the incidents share a perpetrator. The wave follows a similar attack on French supermarkets in October. A store in Lilienthal, Germany, said it had to discard goods worth more than €360,000, while six Romanian stores were affected. Italy’s government held talks with intelligence and cybersecurity officials and said the impact there was limited to a small number of commercial sites; it reported no health risk from thawed food. EU officials are coordinating with national authorities, who are conducting the investigations. Agriculture Commissioner Christophe Hansen said the bloc’s food supply was not currently threatened, and the Commission said the incidents showed a need for stronger cybersecurity across the EU.

items.title: [popsci.com] Nearby giant likely tilted hot Jupiter out of view
items.content_html:
🌾 ✏️

Astronomers say the hot Jupiter TOI-2535 b, about 1,000 light-years away, stopped transiting its star in March 2026 because the gravitational pull of a nearby, still-unseen planet tilted its orbit out of Earth’s line of sight. NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days. Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner.

NASA’s Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite observed the system from April 2019 to March 2026; the planet circles its star every 8.25 days (popsci.com, skyatnightmagazine.com, antena3.ro). Before the transits vanished, they arrived as much as six hours early or late and grew shorter and shallower, signs that the orbit’s alignment was changing. How the planet moved close to its star remains uncertain. The study appeared in *The Astrophysical Journal Letters* on Nov. 9. TOI-2535 b is not expected to transit again for at least 30 years, while its companion could become visible in transit sooner (universetoday.com, stirileprotv.ro, popsci.com). Companion estimate: Analysis using the NEID spectrograph at Arizona’s WIYN telescope points to a companion at least as massive as Saturn, with an orbit tilted at least 5 degrees relative to TOI-2535 b’s (xataka.com). Extreme changes: Researchers describe the system’s variations in transit duration and changes in orbital inclination as the largest measured for a planet around a single star (universetoday.com). Hot-Jupiter rarity: These planets usually lack close, massive companions; TOI-2535 b’s neighbor may itself be a short-period giant, unlike most known hot-Jupiter companions (universetoday.com).
items._kite_context:
Quote: "We think of the universe as resembling clockwork, where everything is regular, but that’s not true." (Samuel Yee, University of California, Los Angeles postdoctoral fellow and study corresponding author, Futurism)
Timeline: April 2019: TESS observations of TOI-2535 b began (skyatnightmagazine.com, antena3.ro).
Timeline: March 2026: TESS no longer detected the planet’s characteristic transits (antena3.ro, stirileprotv.ro).
Timeline: 9 November 2026: The study of the disappearing transits appeared in The Astrophysical Journal Letters (stirileprotv.ro).
Background: Other mechanisms have also been linked to disappearing or changing exoplanet transits: Kepler-413b stopped transiting for 800 days under the influence of its two stars, while TOI-1518b’s orbital orientation is expected to shift because of its star’s shape
